get-or-default.why: getOrDefault returns the value for the key if there is one, otherwise the default you pass in. That's what makes it handy for counting: no null check needed.

count-banana.why: Each character's count starts at 0 via getOrDefault and goes up by one. A TreeMap keeps its keys sorted, so the map prints in the order a, b, n.

count-fill.why: counts.getOrDefault(c, 0) reads the current count, using 0 the first time c appears; adding one and putting it back updates the count.

count-steps.why: You need the map before you can fill it, the characters before you can loop over them, and the counts before you can return them.

fast-lookup.why: Hash-based structures find a key in constant time on average. TreeMap is a balanced tree, so lookups are O(log n), and ArrayList.contains scans the list, O(n).

string-identity.why: == compares references: whether both variables point at the same object. Two separately built Strings with equal characters are different objects; compare their contents with equals.

triangular-loop.why: The inner loop runs 0, 1, 2, …, n−1 times: n(n−1)/2 in total. Halving the work still grows with n², so it's O(n²).

doubling-loop.why: i doubles every step (1, 2, 4, 8, …), so it passes n after about log₂ n steps.

longest-unique-run.why: It asks about a contiguous region (a substring) with a constraint you can maintain as it grows and shrinks (no repeats), which is the sliding-window cue: O(n). Checking every substring works but is O(n³) or O(n²). Sorting destroys the order that defines a substring, and there's no monotone condition to binary search on the first repeat.
